message.content:
Here are some popular sushi restaurants in Tokyo that are well‑known among locals and visitors alike:

| Restaurant | Location | Highlights |
|------------|----------|-------------|
| **Sukiyabashi Jiro** | Ginza (Tokyo Station area) | Legendary chef Jiro Ono; Michelin‑starred; famous for its meticulous preparation and high price point. |
| **Sushi Saito** | Ginza | Three Michelin stars; extremely small seating capacity; known for its intimate setting and impeccable quality. |
| **Sushi Yoshitake** | Ginza | Two Michelin stars; focuses on seasonal ingredients and a refined tasting menu. |
| **Sushi Dai** | Tsukiji Outer Market | Renowned for fresh tuna; long lines but worth the wait for a classic Tsukiji experience. |
| **Sushi Daiwa** | Tsukiji Outer Market | Similar to Sushi Dai; offers a slightly different selection of nigiri and sashimi. |
| **Sushi Kyubey** | Ginza | Classic sushi spot with a reputation for consistency and high‑quality fish. |
| **Sushi Sugimoto** | Ginza | Known for its “sushi bar” style, allowing diners to watch chefs at work. |
| **Sushi Sawada** | Ginza | One Michelin star; praised for its creative rolls and attentive service. |
| **Sushi Masuda** | Ginza | Small, intimate setting; focuses on traditional Edomae sushi techniques. |
| **Sushi Shikon** | Ginza | Two Michelin stars; offers a tasting menu that showcases seasonal ingredients. |
| **Sushi Kanda** | Ginza | Three Michelin stars; known for its meticulous presentation and high level of craftsmanship. |
| **Sushi Iwa** | Ginza | One Michelin star; offers a more relaxed atmosphere while still delivering top‑notch sushi. |
| **Sushi Takuya** | Ginza | Two Michelin stars; known for its innovative approach to sushi and sashimi. |
